claim: CFTR is the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients.
source: In CFTR, the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, ATP-binding-induced dimerization of two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) opens the pore, and dimer disruption following ATP hydrolysis closes it.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CFTR's role in cystic fibrosis.

claim: ATP-binding-induced dimerization of two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) opens the CFTR pore.
source: In CFTR, the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, ATP-binding-induced dimerization of two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) opens the pore, and dimer disruption following ATP hydrolysis closes it.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism, supported by prior research.

claim: Dimer disruption following ATP hydrolysis closes the CFTR pore.
source: In CFTR, the chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, ATP-binding-induced dimerization of two cytosolic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) opens the pore, and dimer disruption following ATP hydrolysis closes it.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism.

claim: Spontaneous openings without ATP are rare in wild-type CFTR.
source: Spontaneous openings without ATP are rare in wild-type CFTR, but in certain CF mutants constitute the only gating mechanism, stimulated by ivacaftor, a clinically approved CFTR potentiator.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in the manuscript and prior knowledge.

claim: In certain CF mutants, spontaneous openings constitute the only gating mechanism.
source: Spontaneous openings without ATP are rare in wild-type CFTR, but in certain CF mutants constitute the only gating mechanism, stimulated by ivacaftor, a clinically approved CFTR potentiator.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CF mutants.

claim: Ivacaftor is a clinically approved CFTR potentiator that stimulates spontaneous openings.
source: Spontaneous openings without ATP are rare in wild-type CFTR, but in certain CF mutants constitute the only gating mechanism, stimulated by ivacaftor, a clinically approved CFTR potentiator.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the drug ivacaftor.

claim: Spontaneous openings are strictly coupled to NBD dimerization.
source: We show that spontaneous openings are also strictly coupled to NBD dimerization, which may therefore occur even without ATP.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from mutant cycle analysis.

claim: NBD dimerization may occur even without ATP.
source: We show that spontaneous openings are also strictly coupled to NBD dimerization, which may therefore occur even without ATP.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that spontaneous openings are coupled to NBD dimerization.

claim: Coordinated NBD/pore movements are intrinsic to CFTR.
source: Coordinated NBD/pore movements are therefore intrinsic to CFTR: ATP alters the stability, but not the fundamental structural architecture, of open- and closed-pore conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing coupling in both ATP-dependent and spontaneous gating.

claim: ATP alters the stability, but not the fundamental structural architecture, of open- and closed-pore conformations.
source: Coordinated NBD/pore movements are therefore intrinsic to CFTR: ATP alters the stability, but not the fundamental structural architecture, of open- and closed-pore conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar coupling patterns with and without ATP.

claim: CFTR belongs to the superfamily of ATP binding cassette (ABC) proteins.
source: The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) is a chloride ion channel which belongs to the superfamily of ATP binding cassette (ABC) proteins (Riordan et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riordan et al., 1989.

claim: Following phosphorylation of the cytosolic regulatory (R) domain by cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA), CFTR channels are gated by cytosolic ATP.
source: Following phosphorylation of the cytosolic regulatory (R) domain by cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA), CFTR channels are gated by cytosolic ATP (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR regulation, supported by Figure 1a.

claim: The ion pore within the TMDs opens upon formation of a tight head-to-tail NBD dimer stabilized by two molecules of ATP occluded at the dimer interface.
source: The ion pore within the TMDs opens upon formation of a tight head-to-tail NBD dimer stabilized by two molecules of ATP occluded at the dimer interface (Vergani et al., 2005); each nucleotide is sandwiched between the conserved Walker A and B sequences of one NBD and the signature sequence of the other (Smith et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vergani et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2003.

claim: Each nucleotide is sandwiched between the conserved Walker A and B sequences of one NBD and the signature sequence of the other.
source: The ion pore within the TMDs opens upon formation of a tight head-to-tail NBD dimer stabilized by two molecules of ATP occluded at the dimer interface (Vergani et al., 2005); each nucleotide is sandwiched between the conserved Walker A and B sequences of one NBD and the signature sequence of the other (Smith et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2003.

claim: Pore closure accompanies NBD dimer disruption prompted by ATP hydrolysis at the composite interfacial site harbouring the Walker motifs of NBD2 (site 2).
source: Pore closure accompanies NBD dimer disruption prompted by ATP hydrolysis at the composite interfacial site harbouring the Walker motifs of NBD2 (site 2) (Vergani et al., 2005): the other site (site 1) is catalytically inactive retaining ATP bound throughout multiple gating cycles (Aleksandrov et al., 2002; Basso et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: Site 1 is catalytically inactive retaining ATP bound throughout multiple gating cycles.
source: Pore closure accompanies NBD dimer disruption prompted by ATP hydrolysis at the composite interfacial site harbouring the Walker motifs of NBD2 (site 2) (Vergani et al., 2005): the other site (site 1) is catalytically inactive retaining ATP bound throughout multiple gating cycles (Aleksandrov et al., 2002; Basso et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aleksandrov et al., 2002; Basso et al., 2003.

claim: A hydrogen bond between the side chains of NBD2 Walker-A threonine (T1246) and an arginine (R555) adjacent to the NBD1 signature sequence forms in open, but not in closed, channels.
source: As evidence of such strict coupling between NBD and transmembrane domain (TMD) movements, a hydrogen bond between the side chains of NBD2 Walker-A threonine (T1246) and an arginine (R555) adjacent to the NBD1 signature sequence was shown to form in open, but not in closed, channels (Vergani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: Positions T1246 and R555 have co-evolved as a pair.
source: These two positions have co-evolved as a pair (Vergani et al., 2005), and in crystal structures of nucleotide-bound ABC NBD dimers the analogous side chains also form a hydrogen bond, the arginine serving as hydrogen donor and the threonine/serine side chain as acceptor (Smith et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: In crystal structures of nucleotide-bound ABC NBD dimers the analogous side chains to R555 and T1246 form a hydrogen bond, the arginine serving as hydrogen donor and the threonine/serine side chain as acceptor.
source: These two positions have co-evolved as a pair (Vergani et al., 2005), and in crystal structures of nucleotide-bound ABC NBD dimers the analogous side chains also form a hydrogen bond, the arginine serving as hydrogen donor and the threonine/serine side chain as acceptor (Smith et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2003.

claim: Both shortening of the R555 side chain (by mutation R555K) and lengthening of the T1246 side chain (by mutation T1246N) prevent the formation of the stabilizing hydrogen bond.
source: Furthermore, by disturbing proper spacing between the donor and acceptor sites, both shortening of the R555 and lengthening of the T1246 side chains (by single mutations R555K and T1246N, respectively) prevent, whereas the double mutation R555K-T1246N restores, the formation of this stabilizing hydrogen bond (Vergani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: The double mutation R555K-T1246N restores the formation of the stabilizing hydrogen bond.
source: Furthermore, by disturbing proper spacing between the donor and acceptor sites, both shortening of the R555 and lengthening of the T1246 side chains (by single mutations R555K and T1246N, respectively) prevent, whereas the double mutation R555K-T1246N restores, the formation of this stabilizing hydrogen bond (Vergani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: Wild-type CFTR channels open occasionally even in the absence of ATP.
source: Wild-type (WT) CFTR channels open occasionally even in the absence of ATP (Szollosi et al., 2010) (Figure 1a, inset), but it is unclear whether this reflects the occasional spontaneous formation of the NBD dimer (Figure 1b, top), or occasional pore openings independent of NBD dimerization (Figure 1b, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Szollosi et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 1a inset.

claim: Ivacaftor acts by promoting spontaneous, ATP-independent, openings of G551D CFTR, the third most common disease mutant.
source: Moreover, ivacaftor, the only potentiator drug to be approved so far for clinical use in CF patients, acts by promoting such spontaneous, ATP-independent, openings of G551D CFTR, the third most common disease mutant (Bompadre et al., 2007; Jih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bompadre et al., 2007; Jih et al., 2013.

claim: G551D CFTR is the third most common disease mutant.
source: Moreover, ivacaftor, the only potentiator drug to be approved so far for clinical use in CF patients, acts by promoting such spontaneous, ATP-independent, openings of G551D CFTR, the third most common disease mutant (Bompadre et al., 2007; Jih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CF mutations.

claim: Mutations in the third intracellular loop (position 978, between TM helices 8 and 9) strongly enhance spontaneous activity.
source: Recently, mutations in the third intracellular loop (position 978, between TM helices 8 and 9) (Wang et al., 2010), and at the cytosolic end of pore-lining TM helix 6 (position 355) (Wei et al., 2014), were both found to strongly enhance spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations at the cytosolic end of pore-lining TM helix 6 (position 355) strongly enhance spontaneous activity.
source: Recently, mutations in the third intracellular loop (position 978, between TM helices 8 and 9) (Wang et al., 2010), and at the cytosolic end of pore-lining TM helix 6 (position 355) (Wei et al., 2014), were both found to strongly enhance spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2014.

claim: The gain-of-function effects of mutations at positions 978 and 355 are additive in the double-mutant P355A–K978C.
source: Furthermore, these 'gain-of-function' effects proved additive in the double-mutant P355A–K978C, shifting spontaneous Po into a range where quantitative biophysical studies become tractable (Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2014.

claim: The P355A-K978C double mutant shifts spontaneous Po into a range where quantitative biophysical studies become tractable.
source: Furthermore, these 'gain-of-function' effects proved additive in the double-mutant P355A–K978C, shifting spontaneous Po into a range where quantitative biophysical studies become tractable (Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2014 and demonstrated by data in the manuscript.

claim: For P355A-K978C CFTR, a readily measurable fraction of the chloride current resisted prolonged removal of bath ATP.
source: Whereas WT CFTR channel currents decline rapidly to baseline upon ATP removal (Figure 1a), in patches containing P355A-K978C CFTR channels (Figure 1c) a readily measurable fraction of the chloride current resisted even prolonged removal of bath ATP, but could be abolished by removal of permeating chloride ions (red bars; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The ATP-independent current in P355A-K978C CFTR could be abolished by removal of permeating chloride ions.
source: Whereas WT CFTR channel currents decline rapidly to baseline upon ATP removal (Figure 1a), in patches containing P355A-K978C CFTR channels (Figure 1c) a readily measurable fraction of the chloride current resisted even prolonged removal of bath ATP, but could be abolished by removal of permeating chloride ions (red bars; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: For WT CFTR, ATP-dependent currents are very small prior to exposure to PKA.
source: Moreover, for WT CFTR, ATP-dependent currents are very small prior to exposure to PKA, and decline by ~50% when PKA is withdrawn (Figure 1a), signalling strong phosphorylation dependence of its Po (Szollosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and supported by citation.

claim: WT CFTR ATP-dependent currents decline by ~50% when PKA is withdrawn.
source: Moreover, for WT CFTR, ATP-dependent currents are very small prior to exposure to PKA, and decline by ~50% when PKA is withdrawn (Figure 1a), signalling strong phosphorylation dependence of its Po (Szollosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: ATP-evoked P355A-K978C CFTR currents were large already before exposure to PKA.
source: In contrast, ATP-evoked P355A-K978C CFTR currents were large already before exposure to PKA, and were little further enhanced by the addition of – or reduced following removal of – the kinase (Figure 1c), suggesting a large Po for unphosphorylated (pre-PKA) double-mutant channels in ATP, and close-to-maximal Po when the channels were either fully phosphorylated (in PKA) or partially dephosphorylated (post-PKA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: ATP-evoked P355A-K978C CFTR currents were little further enhanced by the addition of – or reduced following removal of – PKA.
source: In contrast, ATP-evoked P355A-K978C CFTR currents were large already before exposure to PKA, and were little further enhanced by the addition of – or reduced following removal of – the kinase (Figure 1c), suggesting a large Po for unphosphorylated (pre-PKA) double-mutant channels in ATP, and close-to-maximal Po when the channels were either fully phosphorylated (in PKA) or partially dephosphorylated (post-PKA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: For pre-phosphorylated channels, the P355A-K978C background mutation increased spontaneous Po from 0.000053 ± 0.000021 (n = 5) to 0.15 ± 0.03 (n = 21).
source: Thus, for pre-phosphorylated channels the P355A-K978C background mutation increased spontaneous Po from 0.000053 ± 0.000021 (n = 5) to 0.15 ± 0.03 (n = 21) (Figure 1d, WT vs. BG [background]), and Po in ATP from 0.11 ± 0.04 (n = 6) to 0.80 ± 0.02 (n = 14) (Figure 1d, striped bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The P355A-K978C background mutation increased Po in ATP from 0.11 ± 0.04 (n = 6) to 0.80 ± 0.02 (n = 14).
source: Thus, for pre-phosphorylated channels the P355A-K978C background mutation increased spontaneous Po from 0.000053 ± 0.000021 (n = 5) to 0.15 ± 0.03 (n = 21) (Figure 1d, WT vs. BG [background]), and Po in ATP from 0.11 ± 0.04 (n = 6) to 0.80 ± 0.02 (n = 14) (Figure 1d, striped bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Mutating the arginine at position 555 to a lysine resulted in a large reduction in spontaneous Po to 0.034 ± 0.007 (n = 18).
source: Mutating either the arginine at position 555 to a lysine, or the threonine at position 1246 to an asparagine, resulted in a large reduction in spontaneous Po (Figure 2b–c 0.034 ± 0.007 (n = 18) and 0.044 ± 0.009 (n = 19), respectively, Figure 2e, blue and red bar), that is, in the closed-open equilibrium constant in the absence of ATP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2b-c and 2e.

claim: Mutating the threonine at position 1246 to an asparagine resulted in a large reduction in spontaneous Po to 0.044 ± 0.009 (n = 19).
source: Mutating either the arginine at position 555 to a lysine, or the threonine at position 1246 to an asparagine, resulted in a large reduction in spontaneous Po (Figure 2b–c 0.034 ± 0.007 (n = 18) and 0.044 ± 0.009 (n = 19), respectively, Figure 2e, blue and red bar), that is, in the closed-open equilibrium constant in the absence of ATP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2b-c and 2e.

claim: The double mutant R555K-T1246N displayed a high spontaneous Po of 0.11 ± 0.02 (n = 20), comparable to that of the background construct.
source: In stark contrast to the single mutants, the double mutant R555K-T1246N (Figure 2d) displayed a high spontaneous Po (0.11 ± 0.02 (n = 20); Figure 2e, violet bar), comparable to that of the background construct.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2d and 2e.

claim: A stabilizing interaction, consistent with the formation of a hydrogen bond, exists in the spontaneous open state in WT channels that is lost in both single mutants R555K and T1246N, but is restored in the double mutant.
source: Thus, the only plausible explanation is a stabilizing interaction, consistent with the formation of a hydrogen bond, in the spontaneous open state in WT channels that is lost in both single mutants, but is restored in the double mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant cycle analysis data.

claim: The NBD dimer interface must tighten within site 2 upon pore opening, whether or not bound ATP is present.
source: The inevitable implication of these findings is that the NBD dimer interface must tighten within site 2 upon pore opening, whether or not bound ATP is present.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing interaction changes during spontaneous gating.

claim: The reduced spontaneous open probabilities of both single mutants R555K and T1246N were caused predominantly by a markedly reduced opening rate.
source: Kinetic analysis revealed that the reduced spontaneous open probabilities of both single mutants R555K and T1246N (Figure 2e, blue and red bar) were caused predominantly by a markedly reduced opening rate (Figure 2f, blue and red bar), which was restored in the double mutant (Figure 2f, violet bar).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2e and 2f.

claim: The opening rate was restored in the double mutant R555K-T1246N.
source: Kinetic analysis revealed that the reduced spontaneous open probabilities of both single mutants R555K and T1246N (Figure 2e, blue and red bar) were caused predominantly by a markedly reduced opening rate (Figure 2f, blue and red bar), which was restored in the double mutant (Figure 2f, violet bar).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The change in coupling free energy between the target side chains upon reaching the transition state from the closed state is ΔΔGint(T−C) = –2.30 ± 0.46 kT, which is statistically significant (p = 0.0001).
source: Consequently, a significant (p = 0.0001) negative value of –2.30 ± 0.46 kT (Figure 2i, center) was obtained for the change in coupling free energy between the target side chains upon reaching the transition state from the closed state (ΔΔGint(T−C)).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental kinetic data and shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Closing rates were little affected by the mutations R555K, T1246N, and R555K-T1246N.
source: In contrast, closing rates were little affected by the mutations (Figure 2g), yielding a value of +0.62 ± 0.34 kT for ΔΔGint(T−O), not significantly different from zero (Figure 2j, center).
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The value of ΔΔGint(T−O) is +0.62 ± 0.34 kT, not significantly different from zero.
source: In contrast, closing rates were little affected by the mutations (Figure 2g), yielding a value of +0.62 ± 0.34 kT for ΔΔGint(T−O), not significantly different from zero (Figure 2j, center).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental kinetic data and shown in Figure 2j.

claim: In WT channels the hydrogen bond between the R555 and T1246 side chains is already formed in the transition state for spontaneous opening.
source: These results imply that in WT channels the hydrogen bond between the R555 and T1246 side chains is already formed in the transition state for spontaneous opening, its strength being little further altered when the protein reaches the stable open state (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing coupling changes.

claim: The strength of the hydrogen bond between R555 and T1246 is little further altered when the protein reaches the stable open state from the transition state.
source: These results imply that in WT channels the hydrogen bond between the R555 and T1246 side chains is already formed in the transition state for spontaneous opening, its strength being little further altered when the protein reaches the stable open state (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing minimal change in ΔΔGint(T−O).

claim: The NBD dimer interface tightens within site 2 already in the transition state for unliganded opening.
source: Thus, the NBD dimer interface tightens within site 2 already in the transition state for unliganded opening (Figure 3a, center), just as it does during the opening of ATP-bound channels (Vergani et al., 2005; Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: The NBD dimer interface tightens within site 2 during the opening of ATP-bound channels.
source: Thus, the NBD dimer interface tightens within site 2 already in the transition state for unliganded opening (Figure 3a, center), just as it does during the opening of ATP-bound channels (Vergani et al., 2005; Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vergani et al., 2005; Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: ATP-driven CFTR pore openings are coupled to the formation of a tight NBD dimer.
source: While ATP-driven CFTR pore openings are known to be coupled to the formation of a tight NBD dimer (Vergani et al., 2005), the mechanism of spontaneous openings, observable in the absence of ATP, is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergani et al., 2005.

claim: Spontaneous openings are linked to tightening of the NBD interface around composite site 2, just as in the presence of bound ATP.
source: Here we show that spontaneous openings are also linked to tightening of the NBD interface around composite site 2, just as in the presence of bound ATP.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The G551D CF mutation converts ATP at site 2 into an inhibitory ligand, due to electrostatic repulsion between the γ-phosphate of ATP bound to the Walker motifs, and the introduced negative charge in the signature sequence.
source: For example, the G551D CF mutation converts ATP at site 2 into an inhibitory ligand, due to electrostatic repulsion between the γ-phosphate of ATP bound to the Walker motifs, and the introduced negative charge in the signature sequence (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2014.

claim: Low-probability ATP-independent pore openings of a CFTR construct lacking NBD2 (CFTR residues 1–1197) can clearly not be linked to NBD dimer formation.
source: Furthermore, although reported low-probability ATP-independent pore openings of a CFTR construct lacking NBD2 (CFTR residues 1–1197; [Wang et al., 2007]) can clearly not be linked to NBD dimer formation, the present results argue that upon pore opening its remaining NBD-TMD coupling machinery undergoes movements similar to those that accompany NBD dimerization when neither 'limb' is truncated.
evidence: This is inferred from the citation to Wang et al., 2007 and logical reasoning.

claim: The ATP binding sites of open CFTR channels are likely inaccessible to the bulk solution even in the absence of bound ATP, just as in its presence.
source: Because of the tightened NBD interface, the ATP binding sites of open CFTR channels are likely inaccessible to the bulk solution even in the absence of bound ATP, just as in its presence (Chaves and Gadsby, 2015), suggesting that ATP binding/unbinding can take place only in the closed-channel state.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citation to Chaves and Gadsby, 2015.

claim: ATP binding/unbinding can take place only in the closed-channel state.
source: Because of the tightened NBD interface, the ATP binding sites of open CFTR channels are likely inaccessible to the bulk solution even in the absence of bound ATP, just as in its presence (Chaves and Gadsby, 2015), suggesting that ATP binding/unbinding can take place only in the closed-channel state.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that ATP binding sites are inaccessible in open channels.

claim: The ATP-free open-channel state is unlikely to be an integral component of the ATP-dependent gating cycle.
source: Two immediate corollaries ensue. First, the ATP-free open-channel state is unlikely to be an integral component of the ATP-dependent gating cycle (Szollosi et al., 2010; but, cf. Jih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that ATP binding sites are inaccessible in open channels, supported by citations.

claim: The principles that drive gating of CFTR channels are fundamentally different from those of ligand-gated channels, such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
source: Second, despite suggested similarities (Wang et al., 2010; Kirk et al., 2011; Okeyo et al., 2013), the principles that drive gating of CFTR channels are fundamentally different from those of ligand-gated channels, such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanistic differences and supported by citations.

claim: In ligand-gated channels, ligand binding/unbinding can occur both in the closed- and the open-channel state.
source: Ligand-gated channels obey cyclic equilibrium mechanisms in which ligand binding/unbinding can occur both in the closed- and the open-channel state, and the activating effect of the ligand is based on the thermodynamic principle of detailed balance which constrains the product of the equilibrium constants around a cycle to be unity: thus, opening ('isomerization') is driven by the concurrent conformational change of the ligand binding site which increases its affinity for the ligand (Grosman and Auerbach, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ligand-gated channels, supported by citation to Grosman and Auerbach, 2001.

claim: In CFTR the ligand binding site is occluded in open channels, so that an open-state 'binding affinity' cannot be defined.
source: But in CFTR the ligand binding site is occluded in open channels, so that an open-state 'binding affinity' cannot be defined (the rates for both ATP binding and unbinding are zero).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing inaccessibility of binding sites in open channels.

claim: When disruption of ATP hydrolysis forces CFTR channels to gate at equilibrium, that gating follows a reversible linear sequence, rather than a cycle subject to the principle of detailed balance.
source: Thus, even when disruption of ATP hydrolysis forces CFTR channels to gate at equilibrium, that gating follows a reversible linear sequence (cf., Figure 3a), rather than a cycle subject to the principle of detailed balance.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanistic understanding and illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: Both unliganded and liganded Po is increased by R-domain phosphorylation, presumably by altering R-domain interactions with the TMDs.
source: For instance, both unliganded and liganded Po is increased in a physiological context by R-domain phosphorylation, presumably by altering R-domain interactions with the TMDs (Wang et al., 2010), or in a therapeutic context by the CF drug ivacaftor, believed to target the TMDs (Jih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2010; Jih et al., 2013.

claim: Both unliganded and liganded Po is increased by the CF drug ivacaftor, believed to target the TMDs.
source: For instance, both unliganded and liganded Po is increased in a physiological context by R-domain phosphorylation, presumably by altering R-domain interactions with the TMDs (Wang et al., 2010), or in a therapeutic context by the CF drug ivacaftor, believed to target the TMDs (Jih et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jih et al., 2013.

claim: Distinct mutations in intracellular loops increase Po for both unliganded and liganded CFTR.
source: Further, distinct mutations in intracellular loops increase (Wang et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2014) or decrease (Wang et al., 2014) Po for both unliganded and liganded CFTR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2014.

claim: Distinct mutations in intracellular loops decrease Po for both unliganded and liganded CFTR.
source: Further, distinct mutations in intracellular loops increase (Wang et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2014) or decrease (Wang et al., 2014) Po for both unliganded and liganded CFTR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The inherent open-channel-state structure is similarly organized in the absence or presence of ATP.
source: The present results suggest a simple, unified explanation for all these findings: energetic stabilization or destabilization of the inherent open-channel-state structure (Figure 3a, right), which we show here is similarly organized in the absence or presence of ATP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: The gain-of-function mutations P355A-K978C stabilize the transition state by ~4.8 kT.
source: Together, these data imply that these gain-of-function mutations stabilize the transition state by far less (only by ~4.8 kT; Figure 3c, left black arrow) than the open state, as expected for perturbations that affect protein positions which have not yet reached their fully open-like conformations in the transition state.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The pore is likely still closed in the high-energy evanescent transition state for spontaneous openings.
source: Thus, just as for ATP-bound channels, the pore is likely still closed in the high-energy evanescent transition state for spontaneous openings (Figure 3a, center cartoon).
evidence: This is inferred from the energetic data and illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: ATP-induced openings are terminated by ATP hydrolysis.
source: Because ATP-induced openings are terminated by ATP hydrolysis (Csanády et al., 2010), energetic interpretation of ATP-binding induced gating effects cannot be based on the comparison of WT gating in the presence and absence of ATP (Figure 1d, WT+ATP vs. WT).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations that disrupt ATP hydrolysis in site 2 all prolong τb and reduce CFTR gating to an equilibrium.
source: Mutations that disrupt ATP hydrolysis in site 2 all prolong τb and reduce CFTR gating to an equilibrium, by forcing the channels to close back through the same high-energy transition state they had traversed upon opening (cf. Figure 3a) (Vergani et al., 2005; Csanády et al., 2010; Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vergani et al., 2005; Csanády et al., 2010; Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: Although the NBD interface is already tightened within site 2 in the ATP-bound transition state, the 'molecular glue' effect of bound ATP is further strengthened when the channel reaches the stable open state.
source: Thus, intriguingly, although the NBD interface is already tightened within site 2 in the ATP-bound transition state (Vergani et al., 2005; Sorum et al., 2015), the 'molecular glue' effect of bound ATP is further strengthened when the channel reaches the stable open state.
evidence: This is inferred from the energetic calculations and supported by citations.

claim: Some rearrangements must still occur within the dimer interface between the transition state and the open state.
source: The implication is that some rearrangements must still occur within the dimer interface between the transition state and the open state.

claim: Oocytes were isolated from anaesthetized adult female Xenopus laevis frogs following Institutional Animal Care Committee guidelines.
